chunks.text: Op-ed · June 7, twenty twenty-six · 6 min read · By Don Goldstein

The temporary streateries that carried so many DC rooms through four summers are gone, and the permanent program is not cheap. If you lost sidewalk seats, the covers do not have to vanish with them — they move indoors and online.
DC's temporary streateries have ended; the permanent DDOT program charges 20 dollars per square foot in road rent plus permits.
Counts are a moving target, but roughly half of the city's ~140 streateries did not survive — many operators lost seats at the summer peak.
Recover the covers indoors: tighten the reservation link, fix the Google profile and photos, and capture overflow with a waitlist.

For four summers, the streatery out front was the difference between a full Friday and a half-empty one. That era is over in DC. The temporary program that let restaurants throw seating into the curb lane has ended, and the permanent replacement that took its place in December twenty twenty-five charges 20 dollars per square foot in “road rent” on top of permits and design rules. Of the roughly 140 streateries the city had, a large share did not come back — and plenty of operators lost real seats just as the summer peak arrives.
If that is you, the covers don’t have to vanish with the seats. They move — indoors, and online — but only if your reservation flow and your Google Business Profile are set up to catch them.

The permanent DDOT program is a real program, not a ban — but it prices and regulates what used to be free and improvised. Per-square-foot road rent, application and permit fees, and design standards turn a streatery into a capital decision rather than a few barriers and a weekend build. By spring, dozens of operators had applied and the city had pulled dozens more; DDOT framed roughly half surviving as a win. The translation for you is simpler: the demand didn’t leave the neighborhood — the seating did. Whoever catches that demand fastest keeps it.
Three moves turn a curb-seat loss into recovered covers. None of them require a permit.

Three moves that turn lost streatery seats into recovered covers. One: tighten the reservation path — the walk-up who used to grab a patio table now needs a fast, mobile reservation link above the fold to book inside instead. Two: fix the profile for the new reality — update hours and the outdoor-seating attribute, and swap the patio photos for the room you actually seat now, so the map shows what is true. Three: capture the overflow — a waitlist or a notify-me on a booked night keeps the cover instead of sending it down the block.

Run the storefront health check the way a diner on a phone would, and the G B P grader to confirm the profile reflects the seats you actually have. The booking side is covered in recovering reservations from Find a Table . The streatery is gone. The summer isn’t.
The 20 dollars/sq-ft road rent is the firm number; the survival count is directional, per Axios and DDOT.
The demand did not leave the neighborhood — the seating did, so whoever catches it fastest keeps it.
A fast mobile reservation link above the fold is the single highest-leverage recovery move.
Update the outdoor-seating attribute and patio photos so the map reflects the seats you actually have.
